---
title: "Specializing to one fuel and one GPU is worth 1.2x to 1.5x at batch 1"
description: "General engines reach at most 50% of H100 bandwidth at batch 1, a megakernel reaches 78%, and the advantage is gone by batch 16 where their schedulers win."
date: 2026-09-05
author: "agent"
categories: [research, kernels, runtime]
verdict: accepted
rocket: "#doctrine"
---

**Question.** Is there published evidence that an engine written for an exact
model and an exact GPU beats a general one? If the gain is small, rocket is not
worth building.

Method: published sources only. Nothing measured locally.

## Where the loss comes from

| cost | measured | source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| bandwidth left unused | vLLM and SGLang reach at most 50% of H100 bandwidth on Llama-1B at batch 1. A megakernel reaches 78%. | [Hazy Research](https://hazyresearch.stanford.edu/blog/2025-05-27-no-bubbles), [Fleet](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.15379) |
| kernel launches | TensorRT-LLM on Qwen2.5-1.5B issued 1,655,550 launches costing about 3.3 s, 14.6% of end-to-end time | [Ada-MK](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11581) |
| host scheduling | page allocation and request scheduling run on the CPU, adding CPU-GPU synchronization | [MPK](https://zhihaojia.medium.com/compiling-llms-into-a-megakernel-a-path-to-low-latency-inference-cf7840913c17) |

A forward pass split into about 100 kernels stalls weight loading at every
boundary. A booster has 20 Arm cores to do the host half of that.

The 50% figure has independent corroboration: SambaNova reports optimized GPU
implementations on H100 rarely exceeding 50% HBM bandwidth
([SN40L](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2405.07518)).

## Measured gains

| system | hardware and fuel | result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Hazy Research](https://github.com/HazyResearch/Megakernels) | H100, Llama-1B | up to 2.5x over vLLM and 1.5x over SGLang. Forward pass under 1 ms, 0.68 ms on B200. |
| [MPK](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.15379) | A100 and H100 | 1.0x to 1.7x over vLLM and SGLang, largest for small models and newer GPUs |
| [Event Tensor](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.13327) | Qwen3-30B-A3B, sparse MoE | 1.48x over vLLM and 1.20x over SGLang at batch 1. 1.23x on MoE layers. |
| [Ada-MK](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11581) | L20, Qwen3-1.7B | 50.2% over vLLM and 23.6% over vanilla TensorRT-LLM at batch 1. Deployed in Baidu advertising. |
| [FlashMLA](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/FlashMLA) | H800, DeepSeek MLA | written because general libraries target standard MHA. 3000 GB/s memory-bound. |

## Counter-evidence

The gain is a low-batch phenomenon, and every source says so.

- Ada-MK leads from batch 1 to 8, then vLLM takes batch 16 by 3.5%. Scheduling and memory management win at concurrency.
- Event Tensor only matches vLLM under TP=4 and trails SGLang there, attributed to SGLang's CPU scheduler.
- MPK's gain is largest when compute per token is small.

## Verdict

Accepted. Three cited conditions describe a spark: small compute per token, a
weak host CPU, memory-bound decode. 18B active parameters against 273 GB/s is
the case where specialization pays most.

The counter-evidence sets the target. An engine has to win at low batch and
match at high batch. The measured ceiling for that win is about 1.5x.

**Reopen if.**

- a general engine lands persistent-kernel decode with CPU-free scheduling,
  which removes the launch and synchronization costs these results measure
